corpus_definition: the act of causing great physical or mental pain on purpose

forms.definition: the act of hurting someone very badly on purpose
forms.example: The use of torture is forbidden under international law.

syn.note: Cruelty is any behaviour that causes pain; this word is for very strong, planned pain.
Abuse is cruel or wrong treatment in general, not always so extreme.
Agony is the very strong pain a person feels, not the act of causing it.

forms.definition: to hurt someone very badly on purpose, often to get information
forms.example: The prisoners were tortured until they gave the names.

syn.note: Close in meaning; often used for mental pain or for annoying someone again and again.
Easy, general word for causing pain; much weaker.
To treat someone in a cruel or wrong way; not always so extreme.

forms.definition: showing or suffering great pain or worry
forms.example: He had a tortured look on his face after the bad news.

syn.note: Showing very strong pain or worry; a bit formal.
Feeling pain, but not always so strongly.

forms.definition: causing a lot of pain or suffering
forms.example: The long wait at the hospital was torturous.

syn.note: Easy word with a similar meaning, but less strong.
Very close; British spelling: agonising.

forms.note: There is no common adverb made from torture.

people.definition: a person who hurts people badly on purpose
people.example: The torturer was sent to prison for many years.

context.text: In the old prison museum, you can read about the torture of prisoners long ago. Guards tortured people to get names. Today such acts are forbidden by law.

reviewer_note: Kept the act-of-causing-pain sense; tortured (adjective) and torturous are both learner-dictionary words.

corpus_definition: Something that is poisonous and can kill you.

forms.definition: how poisonous or harmful something is
forms.example: Scientists tested the toxicity of the river water.

syn.note: How much harm something can do, not only by poison.

forms.note: There is no verb made from toxic.

forms.definition: poisonous and able to make you very ill or kill you
forms.example: Do not drink from that bottle as it is toxic.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common in everyday English.
Can hurt you, but not always by poison.
Able to kill; used for poison, weapons and diseases.
Easy, general word: it can hurt you in any way.

ant.note: Easy word: it will not hurt you.

forms.note: There is no common adverb made from toxic.

people.definition: a poisonous substance, often made by plants, animals or germs
people.example: Some mushrooms contain a toxin that can kill you.

context.text: The factory near the river was closed because it put toxic waste into the water. Now scientists check the toxicity of the fish every month.

reviewer_note: Intoxicate shares an old root but means 'make drunk' and is not made from toxic, so it is listed in not_family.

corpus_definition: To follow the path or location of something.

forms.definition: marks on the ground that show where a person, animal or car went
forms.example: We followed the fox's tracks in the snow.
forms.note: Also used in 'keep track of' = know where something is. Other meanings: a race path, a song on an album.

syn.note: Marks or signs left by someone moving; very close.
The mark of one foot or shoe only.
A way to walk along, not the marks someone left.

forms.definition: the act of following where something or someone is, often with GPS
forms.example: The delivery app has live tracking, so I know when my food will arrive.

syn.note: Watching something over time; a bit more formal.

forms.definition: to follow where something or someone goes or is
forms.example: I can track my order on the website.

syn.note: Easy word; track often means using a map, app or marks on the ground.
To find where someone or something is or went, often after searching.
To follow someone secretly, often by the marks they leave.
To watch something carefully over time; more formal.

ant.note: To no longer know where something is: 'I lost him in the crowd.'

forms.note: There is no common adjective made from track in this meaning.
There is no adverb made from track.

people.definition: a small device or app that shows where something or someone is
people.example: She put a tracker on her suitcase before the flight.
people.note: Also a person who follows animals by their marks.

context.text: I ordered a new phone online and tracked the parcel every day. The tracking page showed it was already in Samarkand, so I went to the post office.

reviewer_note: Verb sense = follow the location; noun track kept as marks on the ground (same idea), race track and music track are other meanings.

corpus_definition: The act of buying and selling goods.

forms.definition: the buying and selling of goods between people or countries
forms.example: International trade helps countries grow.
forms.note: Another meaning: a job that needs skill with your hands, such as building.

syn.note: Same idea, more formal; used about business in general.
Easy, wider word for making and selling things.
Giving one thing and getting another; not always for money.

forms.definition: the activity of buying and selling, especially shares or goods
forms.example: Trading on the stock market stopped early because of the news.

syn.note: Buying and selling, often of one kind of goods.

forms.definition: to buy and sell goods, or to exchange things
forms.example: Uzbekistan trades cotton and fruit with many countries.

syn.note: Easy phrase with a similar meaning.
Usually 'deal in' a kind of goods: 'He deals in old cars.'
To give one thing and get another back.
Only one side of it: giving goods for money.

forms.note: There is no common adjective made from trade; it is used as a noun before another noun: a trade route.
There is no adverb made from trade.

people.definition: a person who buys and sells goods, often at a market
people.example: The traders at Chorsu Bazaar open their shops very early.

context.text: Trade along the Silk Road made cities like Bukhara rich. Merchants traded silk, spices and cotton there for hundreds of years.

reviewer_note: Compounds (trademark, tradesman) left out; trade (skilled job) is another meaning, mentioned in the noun note.

corpus_definition: Very sad, often involving death or loss.

forms.definition: a very sad event, often when people die
forms.example: The plane crash was a terrible tragedy for the whole country.
forms.note: Another meaning: a serious play with a sad ending, like Hamlet.

syn.note: A sudden event that causes a lot of damage or death.
A very big disaster; a bit formal.
Bad luck; usually less serious.

forms.note: There is no verb made from tragic.

forms.definition: very sad, often because someone has died
forms.example: It was a tragic accident for everyone.

syn.note: Easy word; tragic is much stronger and usually about death or loss.
Making you feel very sad.
Very bad; not always sad.
Causing great damage or shock.

forms.definition: in a very sad way, often involving death
forms.example: He died tragically young, at only twenty-five.

syn.note: Easy word, but much weaker.
Used to say something bad happened; not so strong.

context.text: The news about the bus accident on the road to Fergana was tragic. Three students died tragically, and the whole town still remembers the tragedy.

reviewer_note: No affix claimed: tragically is tragic + -ally, and removing -ic leaves no real word.

corpus_definition: To shake slightly because of cold or strong feelings.

forms.definition: a small shaking movement, often in the voice or hands
forms.example: There was a tremble in her voice when she spoke.

syn.note: Easy, general word for this movement.
A very small, fast shaking; a bit literary.
Shaking mostly because of cold.

forms.definition: to shake a little because you are cold, afraid or excited
forms.example: My hands began to tremble with fear.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning.
Used mostly when you are cold.
A very small, fast shaking; a bit literary.
One strong shake, often because of fear or disgust.

forms.definition: shaking slightly because of fear, cold or strong feelings
forms.example: She held the letter in her trembling hands.

syn.note: Easy, common word: shaky hands, a shaky voice.
Worried or afraid; you may tremble when you are nervous.

forms.note: There is no common adverb made from tremble.

context.text: It was very cold at the bus stop, and Malika began to tremble. Her trembling hands could not hold the cup of hot tea.

reviewer_note: Tremor comes from the same old root but is not made from tremble; listed in people_not_family.

corpus_definition: To make something start or happen very quickly.

forms.definition: something that makes a problem, feeling or event start
forms.example: Stress can be a trigger for bad headaches.
forms.note: Another meaning: the small part of a gun you pull to fire it.

syn.note: The reason something happens; a trigger is what starts it quickly.
A small thing that starts something bigger.
Formal word for something that makes a body or person react.

forms.definition: to make something start or happen suddenly
forms.example: Loud noises can trigger his bad memories.

syn.note: Phrasal verb with the same meaning: set off an alarm.
Easy, general word; it does not say the start is sudden.
Often used for arguments, protests and ideas.
Often used for a strong reaction, like anger; a bit formal.
Easy word, but more general.

ant.note: To stop something from happening at all.

forms.note: There is no common adjective made from trigger.
There is no adverb made from trigger.

context.text: In spring, the dust and flowers in Tashkent can trigger allergies. For my sister, the main trigger is dust from the street, so she wears a mask.

reviewer_note: Gun-part sense of the noun mentioned in a note only; verb sense = make something start.

corpus_definition: A great success or victory after a difficult situation.

forms.definition: a great win or success after a hard time
forms.example: The athlete enjoyed a great triumph at the Olympics.

syn.note: A win in a fight or game; very close.
Easy, general word; triumph is a very big success.
Easy word, often used for games and sport.
Something good you did with effort.

forms.definition: to win or succeed after a hard fight
forms.example: In the end, good triumphed over evil.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
To do what you wanted to do.
Formal: to win in the end.
To deal with a problem successfully.

forms.definition: very happy and proud because you have won or succeeded
forms.example: The team came home triumphant after the final.

syn.note: Having won; a bit formal.
Pleased with what you did; not always after a win.
Getting what you wanted; less emotional.

forms.definition: made or done to celebrate a great victory
forms.example: The army marched through the triumphal arch.

forms.definition: in a very happy and proud way after winning
forms.example: She smiled triumphantly when she got the top mark.

syn.note: In a proud way; not always after a win.
In a very happy way.

context.text: Winning the national cup was a great triumph for the small team from Namangan. The triumphant players danced on the field, and their fans sang triumphantly all night.

reviewer_note: Triumphant (feeling) vs triumphal (celebrating a victory, e.g. an arch) both shown.

corpus_definition: Groups of soldiers who work for the army.

forms.definition: soldiers, especially a large group of them
forms.example: The troops marched across the field at dawn.
forms.note: Usually plural. Singular troop = a group of soldiers, scouts or animals.

syn.note: Easy word with the same meaning.
An army or armed group; often 'armed forces'.
The whole organisation of soldiers in a country.

forms.definition: to walk somewhere together as a group
forms.example: The children trooped into the classroom after the break.
forms.note: Belongs to troop = a group of people moving together, not soldiers. Informal.
There is no adjective made from troops.
There is no adverb made from troops.

people.definition: a soldier of low rank, or a US state police officer
people.example: A young trooper waved to the children from the truck.

context.text: The troops arrived in the city early in the morning. A young trooper waved to the children who were watching from the road.

reviewer_note: Plural headword: the map keeps troops as the base; singular troop explained in a note.

corpus_definition: Hot and wet regions located near the middle of the world.

forms.definition: the hot, wet parts of the world near the equator
forms.example: Many colourful birds live in the tropics.
forms.note: Usually 'the tropics'. Singular tropic = one of two lines on a map north and south of the equator.

syn.note: The line around the middle of the earth; the hot regions are near it.
A thick, wet forest; many are found in these hot regions.

forms.note: There is no verb made from tropics.

forms.definition: from or like the hot, wet parts of the world
forms.example: We bought tropical fruit like mango and pineapple at the market.

syn.note: Near the equator; more scientific.
Hot and wet (about weather), not only in these regions.
Easy word, only about temperature.

ant.note: From the very cold areas near the North or South Pole.
From the very cold area around the North Pole.

forms.note: There is no common adverb made from tropics.

context.text: My cousin moved from Tashkent to a city in the tropics. She says the tropical rain there is warm and falls almost every afternoon.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: the example sentence does not use the word tropics; the map example uses it.
